provenance: SECURIUM_INDEPENDENTLY_AUTHORED; Python/Vibe review summary used only for reauthoring

theory.title: Trust boundaries for AI-assisted Python
theory.summary: Define requirements, identify who controls each value, name the interpreter at each sink, and treat generated code as untrusted until a human verifies it.
theory.pythonExample: Use a typed request object and explicit boundary comments; do not copy generated code directly into a handler.
theory.vibeExample: Prompt for a threat model, assumptions, rejected alternatives, and tests; require the model to label uncertainty.
theory.framework: Use Source / Validation / Sink when the data-flow is concrete; keep prompt provenance and human review as separate controls.

theory.title: Python validation and interpreter separation
theory.summary: Turn feature requirements into type, length, range, and allowlist rules. Bind SQL values, use argument arrays for subprocesses, and never treat eval or exec as a validator.
theory.pythonExample: Prefer re.fullmatch with a feature-specific grammar and subprocess.run([program, arg], shell=False, check=True). Compare literal str.replace with regex-aware re.sub deliberately; do not carry Java replace/replaceAll assumptions into Python.
theory.vibeExample: Ask for negative tests and a rejected-input table before asking for implementation.
theory.framework: Source / Validation / Sink applies when untrusted input crosses a parser, shell, regex, or database boundary.

theory.title: Data access and Python deserialization
theory.summary: Keep values separate from SQL structure, use safe parsers, and reject pickle or unsafe YAML for untrusted data. eval and exec are code execution sinks, not convenience parsers.
theory.pythonExample: Use parameterized DB-API calls and yaml.safe_load for data-shaped YAML; prefer JSON with an allowlisted schema.
theory.vibeExample: Require generated code to name the parser, input trust level, and allowed object types.
theory.framework: Source / Validation / Sink is useful for request bytes to parser to object construction, but parser provenance and integrity assumptions must also be recorded.

theory.title: Filesystem, uploads, and outbound requests
theory.summary: Generated storage names, canonical containment, object authorization, upload limits, and explicit outbound URL policy are required. Host validation alone is not a complete SSRF defense.
theory.pythonExample: Resolve a candidate beneath a fixed base and apply scheme, hostname, IP, redirect, timeout, and egress policy before a request.
theory.vibeExample: Ask the model to produce path and URL edge-case matrices, including false positives and redirect behavior.
theory.framework: Source / Validation / Sink works for filename or URL to filesystem/network sink, provided canonicalization and final-object checks are explicit.

theory.title: Contextual output, CSRF, and safe failure
theory.summary: Encode for the output context, preserve template autoescaping, use CSRF protections when browsers attach credentials, and separate safe client errors from redacted operator telemetry.
theory.pythonExample: Use a framework's escaped text rendering for HTML and a CSRF token or equivalent origin-bound defense for state-changing browser requests.
theory.vibeExample: Require generated examples to show the rendering context and the CSRF threat model, not merely a library call.
theory.framework: Source / Validation / Sink is appropriate for untrusted text to an HTML, URL, header, log, or JSON sink; it does not replace session or authorization analysis.

theory.title: Identity, object authorization, and session state
theory.summary: Authentication identifies a subject; authorization decides whether that subject may perform an action on this object. Enforce the decision server-side and default deny.
theory.pythonExample: Load the object, evaluate policy(actor, object, action), and return a uniform denial without trusting a client role or object ownership claim.
theory.vibeExample: Ask for an owner/member/unrelated/admin matrix and tests that substitute another valid object identifier.
theory.framework: Source / Validation / Sink helps trace identity and object identifiers, but policy authority remains a server-side control.

theory.title: Secrets and dependency decisions
theory.summary: Minimize secret collection, use managed configuration, redact traces, inventory dependencies, review reachability, and protect the build path. Scanner output is a triage signal, not a verdict.
theory.pythonExample: Read a required secret from an approved secret provider and never include it in exception text, logs, prompts, or generated patches.
theory.vibeExample: Instruct the model to omit secrets and lockfile changes unless explicitly reviewed; require an owner and upgrade decision.
theory.framework: Source / Validation / Sink applies to secret sources and log/response sinks, not to proving dependency exploitability.

theory.title: Human verification of AI-generated Python
theory.summary: Use the complete loop: requirements, prompt, generated code, review, tests, repair, and human re-verification. AI output never becomes grading or security authority by itself.
theory.pythonExample: Review a small Python service with a vulnerable, secure, and false-positive fixture for each selected category.
theory.vibeExample: Capture prompt version, generated revision, reviewer decisions, test evidence, residual risk, and rejected suggestions.
theory.framework: Use Source / Validation / Sink only where it clarifies the code path; retain a separate human acceptance decision and provenance record.
